notes.short: Job's friends as the only wise men: said in irony
notes.about: Job seems to grant that his friends are the only wise people, so that wisdom will die with them. He means the opposite, as the next verse says: “I am not inferior to you.” Their speeches had told him nothing he did not know.

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die
figure.means: that his friends were no wiser than he was, for all their claim to teach him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under irony spoken by men: Job's friends had no more knowledge than he. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the words are meant as irony, as if all understanding were theirs alone. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls them ironical, Clarke a strong irony, and Henry says Job speaks ironically of their claim to all wisdom.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: This powerful Irony is meant to emphasise the fact that Job’s friends had no more knowledge than he
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: is intended as irony: ye are not merely single individuals, but the people = race of men ... so that all human understanding is confined to you, and there is none other to be found; and when once you die, it will seem to have died out.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Ironical, as if all the wisdom in the world was concentrated in them and would expire when they expired.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Doubtless ye are the wisest men in the world; all wisdom is concentrated in you; and when ye die, there will no more be found on the face of the earth! This is a strong irony.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He represents them as claiming the monopoly of wisdom ... He speaks ironically: "No doubt you are the people; you think yourselves fit to dictate and give law to all mankind
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Night, then morning; then back to the night
notes.about: Verse 19 can be read as the wicked man's sudden end, either in the night after he lies down, or by day after he opens his eyes. Verse 20 then answers the two crosswise: first terrors like a flood, then a tempest in the night, so the night opens and closes the picture.

lines.words: He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more;
when he opens his eyes, all is gone.
Terrors overtake him like a flood;
a tempest sweeps him away in the night.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) reads verse 19 as sudden death, either in the night after the man lies down rich or by day after he opens his eyes in the morning, and says the two lines of verse 20 are attached crosswise to that picture of destruction by night or by day: the terrors of death seize him like a flood, and by night a whirlwind carries him away.
notes.limit: The first line of verse 20 names no time; it answers the day only by its place in the crossing. Other writers take lying down in verse 19 as dying, not as going to bed, and do not mark this order.

cites.quote: he lieth down to sleep rich, and he doeth it no more, since in the night he is removed from life ... by sudden death; or also: in the morning he openeth his eyes ... he closes them for ever ... attached crosswise (chiastisch) to this picture of sudden destruction, be it by night or by day: the terrors of death seize him ... like a flood ... by night a whirlwind ... carrieth him away
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The realm of the dead speaks of wisdom
notes.about: Abaddon and Death, the world of the dead, are made to speak like persons, as the ocean depths do in verse 14. Even there wisdom is known only by a rumor: they have heard of it, but they do not understand it.

figure.name: Personification
figure.means: the world of the dead, which has only heard a distant report of wisdom

original.note: In Hebrew Abaddon means destruction; here, as in Job 26:6, it names the world of the dead.

notes.evidence: Barnes calls the verse a personification, and an exceedingly sublime one; he takes Abaddon, as in Job 26:6, for the world of the dead, whose deep and dark regions had only heard a distant report of wisdom and did not understand it.

cites.quote: Destruction - This is a personification which is exceedingly sublime. ... see the notes at Job 26:6. It is employed here, as in that place, to denote the nether world - the abode of departed spirits ... The sense is, that those deep and dark regions had simply heard the distant report of wisdom but they did not understand it
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Six troubles, even seven: however many come
notes.about: Eliphaz tells Job that God will rescue him from six calamities, then raises the count to seven. The numbers do not count troubles: they mean that however many come, God is able to deliver from them all.

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven
figure.means: every trouble that may come, however many

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says six is an indefinite number, one more added to mean every case. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a number, then the next higher, for all possible troubles. Clarke: six and seven are put for many. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): formed like the number proverbs, still more than six. Henry: however often troubles come, God delivers out of them all.
notes.limit: These are Eliphaz's words to Job. The note is on how he counts, not on whether his counsel fit Job's case.

cites.quote: Six is used here to denote an indefinite number, meaning that he would support in many troubles. This mode of speech is not uncommon among the Hebrews, where one number is mentioned, so that an extreme number may be immediately added. The method is, to mention a number within the limit, and then to add one more, meaning that in all instances the thing referred to would occur.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Hebrew idiom fixes on a certain number (here "six"), in order to call attention as to a thing of importance; then increases the force by adding, with a "yea, nay seven," the next higher number; here "seven," the sacred and perfect number. In all possible troubles; not merely in the precise number "seven."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The numbers six and seven are put here for many. Though a number of troubles should come upon thee all at once, and there should be no hope, humanly speaking, yet God would rid thee out of them all
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Job 5:19 is formed after the manner of the so-called number-proverbs ... in six troubles, yea in still more than six.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: as afflictions and troubles recur supports and deliverances shall be graciously repeated, be it ever so often ... After six troubles may come a seventh; after many, look for more; but out of them all will God deliver those that are his
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Job's friends fail him like streams that run dry
notes.about: Job says his friends have failed him like desert streams, swollen with ice and snow in winter but gone in the summer heat. The caravans of Tema and Sheba come looking for water and are confounded. So his friends, who came to comfort him, have given him no help.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: my brothers are as faithless as wadis
figure.means: Job's friends, who seemed to promise much comfort and gave none, as streams full in winter fail thirsty travelers in summer

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls the similitude very elegant: the friends' show is the swollen brook, and Job's hope the thirsty traveler's. Albert Barnes calls the simile exquisitely beautiful, Job's hope for comfort like travelers' hope of water. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says Job compares his friends to the swollen wady. Adam Clarke says Job compares them to torrents that soon pass away.
notes.limit: These writers read verse 18 of the streams themselves, wandering from their channels until they come to nothing; the BSB reads it of caravans that turn aside from their routes.

cites.quote: This disappointment which Job met with he here illustrates by the failing of brooks in summer. 1. The similitude is very elegant ... (1.) Their pretensions are fitly compared to the great show which the brooks make when they are swollen with the waters of a land flood
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: I looked for the language of condolence and compassion; for something to cheer my heart, and to uphold me in my trials - as weary and thirsty travelers look for water and are sadly disappointed when they come to the place where they expected to find it, and find the stream dried up. The simile used here is exquisitely beautiful
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Job compares his friends to the wady swollen by ice and snow water, and even to the travelling bands themselves languishing for water. He thirsts for friendly solace, but the seeming comfort which his friends utter is only as the scattered meandering waters in which the mountain brook leaks out.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The approach of Job's friends promised much of sympathy and compassion; his expectations were raised: but their conduct soon convinced him that they were physicians of no value; therefore he compares them to the deceitful torrents that soon pass away.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Job longs for rest like a hired man for evening
notes.about: Job asks whether man's days on earth are not like a hired hand's. A slave longs for the evening shade and a hireling waits for his wages; so Job is allotted months of futility and nights of misery. The point left unsaid is read as Job longing for death as rest after toil.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Like a slave he longs for shade
figure.means: Job himself, who longs for death as rest after hard labor, as a worn-out worker longs for evening and his pay

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls the comparison plain: as a tired servant wishes for evening, so Job wishes for death; Albert Barnes says so too. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the point is that Job waits for death as rest after hard labor. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) asks why, if the servant longs for evening, Job may not long for his hard service to close.
notes.limit: Two of these writers hear in the hireling's wages Job's hope of a reward after this life; the others speak only of rest from toil.

cites.quote: He had as much reason, he thought, to wish for death, as a poor servant or hireling that is tired with his work has to wish for the shadows of the evening, when he shall receive his penny and go to rest ... The comparison is plain, the application is concise and somewhat obscure, but we must supply a word or two, and then it is easy
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The meaning of Job is, that as a servant looked impatiently for the shades of the evening when he would be dismissed from toil, so he longed for death. And as an hireling looketh - That is, he anxiously desires his work to be finished, and expects the reward of his labors. So Job looked to the reward of a life of toil and piety.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The conclusion is intended to be: thus I wait for death as refreshing and rest after hard labour. He goes, however, beyond this next point of comparison, or rather he remains on this side of it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: If the servant longs for the evening when his wages are paid, why may not Job long for the close of his hard service, when he shall enter on his "reward?"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The godless wither like papyrus without water
notes.about: Bildad asks whether papyrus can grow without a marsh, or reeds without water. Without water, they dry up while still green and uncut, quicker than grass. “Such is the destiny of all who forget God”: the godless may flourish for a time, but their hope has no lasting ground and soon perishes.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Such is the destiny of all who forget God
figure.means: the godless, who flourish for a time on ground that cannot last, then wither suddenly, like papyrus cut off from water

notes.evidence: Henry says the hypocrite's hopes are here compared to a rush or flag, which withers before any other herb. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) gives two points of likeness: lush growth, then sudden ruin. Barnes says those who forget God are like the paper-reed, seeming to flourish with nothing firm; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch), that Bildad likens the false ground of their prosperity to it.
notes.limit: These are Bildad's words to Job. The note is on the likeness he draws, not on whether it fit Job's case.

cites.quote: He illustrates this truth by some similitudes. 1. The hopes and joys of the hypocrite are here compared to a rush or flag, ... It withers presently, before any other herb ... The hope of hypocrites is a great cheat upon themselves, and, though it may flourish for a while, it will certainly perish at last, and they with it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Job 8:11-13 embody in poetic and sententious form (probably the fragment of an old poem) the observation of the elders. The double point of comparison between the ungodly and the paper-reed is: 1. the luxuriant prosperity at first; and, 2. the sudden destruction.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: They who forget God are like the paper-reed. They seem to flourish, but they have nothing that is firm and substantial. As the paper-reed soon dies, as the flag withers away before any other herb, so it will be with the wicked, though apparently prosperous.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Bildad likens the deceitful ground on which the prosperity of the godless stands to the dry ground on which, only for a time, the papyrus or reed finds water, and grows up rapidly: shooting up quickly, it withers as quickly
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The godless man as a lush plant torn up
notes.about: Bildad pictures the godless man as a well-watered plant in the sunshine. Its shoots spread over the garden and its roots wrap around the stones, yet once it is uprooted, its place disowns it: “I never saw you.” He thinks his prosperity secure, but it ends suddenly, and others spring up in his place.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: He is a well-watered plant in the sunshine
figure.means: the godless man in his prosperity: spreading and seemingly secure, yet soon torn up and forgotten

notes.evidence: Henry says the hypocrite is here compared to a flourishing, well-rooted tree that is easily cut down. Barnes calls it a new illustration comparing the hypocrite with a quick-growing plant that withers; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the ungodly man is likened to a creeping plant throughout; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), that as the soil disowns the withered weeds, friends disown him.
notes.limit: Writers differ on the kind of plant: a well-rooted tree, a quick-growing plant without depth of root, or a creeper or weeds over stones. These are Bildad's words to Job; the note is on his picture, not on whether it fit Job's case.

cites.quote: The hypocrite is here compared to a flourishing and well-rooted tree, which, though it do not wither of itself, yet will easily be cut down and its place know it no more. ... Thus does a wicked man, when he prospers in the world, think himself secure; his wealth is a high wall in his own conceit.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: A new illustration is here introduced, and the object is to compare the hypocrite with a vigorous plant that grows up quick and sends its branches afar, but which has no depth of root, and which, when the intense heat of the sun comes upon it, withers away.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The subject throughout is not the creeping-plant directly, but the ungodly, who is likened to it. ... As the creeper has stones before it, and by its interwindings, as it were, so rules them that it may call them its own ... so the ungodly regards his fortune as a solid structure, which he has quickly caused to spring up, and which seems to him imperishable.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The very soil is ashamed of the weeds lying withered on its surface, as though it never had been connected with them. So, when the godless falls from prosperity, his nearest friends disown him.

notes.short: Unlike a tree, man is like water that dries up
notes.about: Job sets a man beside a tree. A stump that is cut down can sprout again at the scent of water, “But a man dies and is laid low.” Then he likens a man's death to water that disappears from the sea and a river that dries up: so a man lies down and does not rise.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: As water disappears from the sea
figure.means: a man's death: like water dried up from its bed, he passes from this life and does not come back to it

notes.evidence: Barnes says that as the waters vanish and leave the bed dry, so man passes away and leaves nothing; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), that the dry channel answers to the body laid out in death. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says this vanishing is set under the figure of water that dries up; Henry, that man will not revive as a tree does, and his life may be compared to a land-flood.
notes.limit: Many read the verses as speaking of a return to this life on earth, not as a denial of life to come; verses 13 to 15 go on to hope.

cites.quote: As the waters evaporate wholly, and leave the bottom wholly dry, so it is with man, who passes entirely away, and leaves nothing. ... As such torrents vanish wholly away, so it was with man. Every vestige disappeared
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: fail--utterly disappeared by drying up. The rugged channel of the once flowing water answers to the outstretched corpse ("lieth down," Job 14:12 ) of the once living man.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: How much less favoured is the final lot of man! ... In Job 14:11 . this vanishing away without hope and beyond recovery is contemplated under the figure of running water, or of water that is dried up and never returns again to its channel.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A man cut down by death will not revive again, as a tree cut down will. ... so that the life of man may fitly be compared to the waters of a land-flood, which spread far and make a great show, but they are shallow, and when they are cut off from the sea or river, the swelling and overflowing of which was the cause of them, they soon decay and dry up

notes.short: Evil sweet in the mouth turns to venom inside
notes.about: Zophar pictures evil as sweet food that the wicked man hides under his tongue and will not let go. In his stomach it sours into the venom of cobras; he must vomit up the wealth he swallowed, and the poison kills him. Sin that is pleasant at first comes to a bitter and deadly end.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: Though evil is sweet in his mouth
figure.means: sin, enjoyed and held onto like a sweet morsel, which in the end turns to poison and destroys the one who loved it

notes.evidence: Clarke says verse 12 and the four after it contain an allegory of a man who takes sweet poison for food. Barnes reads them as sin, pleasant at first but bitter in its results; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the evildoer is likened to an epicure; Henry, that such is sin: it turns to the gall of asps; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), that the charm of sin is like sweet poison.
notes.limit: Writers differ on what the sweet morsel stands for most: secret sin, the pleasures of the flesh, or wealth gained by wrong, which verse 15 names. These are Zophar's words to Job; the note is on his picture, not on whether it fit Job's case.

cites.quote: This seems to refer to the secret sins mentioned above. ... This and the four following verses contain an allegory; and the reference is to a man who, instead of taking wholesome food, takes what is poisonous, and is so delighted with it because it is sweet, that he rolls it under his tongue, and will scarcely let it down into his stomach
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Though he has pleasure in committing it, as he has in pleasant food. The sense of this and the following verses is, that though a man may have pleasure in indulgence in sin, and may find happiness of a certain kind in it, yet that the consequences will be bitter - as if the food which he ate should become like gall, and he should cast it up with loathing.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The evil-doer is, in Job 20:12 , likened to an epicure; he keeps hold of wickedness as long as possible, like a delicate morsel that is retained in the mouth ... and seeks to enjoy it to the very last. ... He who sucked in the poison of low desire with a relish, will meet his punishment in that in which he sinned

cites.quote: Sin's fascination is like poison sweet to the taste, but at last deadly to the vital organs
